articles.title: B/R Football Writers' Bold Predictions for the 2026-27 Premier League
articles.summary: And on to the new season of the Premier League.
articles.body:
And on to the new season of the Premier League.

Football's most popular league begins anew on Friday as champions Arsenal begin the defense of their title. Will the Gunners retain their crown? Will opponents Coventry City beat the odds and avoid relegation this season?

Our team of Calum Rogers, Leo Collis and Nick Akerman provided the answers to those questions and more as they offered their bold predictions for the 2026-27 Premier League campaign.

Leo Collis: It should be Erling Haaland. Really, it should. But if we're going for bold predictions, why not pick a striker who scored just three Premier League goals during the whole of last season?

Of course, that description does Alexander Isak a disservice, considering he bagged 54 in 86 top-flight games for Newcastle United across three seasons. But his debut campaign with the Reds was nothing short of disastrous, losing time while being integrated into the XI, sharpening his fitness, and then breaking his leg just as it looked like he was starting to fit in.

That limited him to just 14 games and 702 minutes of action. However, it should be a much different story in 2026-27. Despite a slightly late start because of the World Cup, the Swede actually had a pre-season with the Reds this time around, allowing him to develop more chemistry with his teammates.

Isak has looked sharp in friendly fixtures, and if he can maintain his fitness, he should get back to the levels that saw him notch 21 goals and 23 goals in back-to-back Premier League seasons before his switch to Anfield.

Nick Akerman: This isn't bold in the slightest. I'm sorry. Maybe just offering a plain retort to Leo's argument can be considered bold in the context of this article? It's a cop-out, but I can't in good conscience put forward another player who will even get close to what I expect Haaland to score next season.

Perhaps that's the bold bit? I can realistically see Haaland scoring more than 30 goals, and nobody else even reaching 20. Let's go with that…Manchester City won't win the title, and Haaland will score 15 more than anybody else. Why not?

Calum Rogers: I did consider Igor Thiago and Alexander Isak here, but former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha summed this category up nicely on The Ripple Effect with James Lawrence Allcott : "You can say that Haaland's not gonna score as many, but who's gonna score more?"

And let's not pretend there aren't significant concerns around Haaland's competitors. Isak suffered a broken leg and other muscle issues last season, limiting his impact. Thiago, meanwhile, scored 22 goals last season, but just six of those came in 2026, and eight of his 22 tallies were penalties.

Even if City do fall off considerably under Maresca, it's still tough to imagine Haaland not being able to stay ahead of the competition. He hasn't scored fewer than 22 goals in a season since he was 18, though, so the bold prediction I (a coward) am willing to make is that Haaland will score 21 goals exactly to win the trophy.

Premier League Teams That Will Qualify for the UEFA Champions League

Leo Collis: With Chelsea, my mildly wild pick for Premier League winners, we've got three Champions League spots left to fill—ignoring any additional places awarded to English sides ahead of the 2027-28 tournament.

I'm predicting a bit of a drop-off from Manchester City, who will suffer a Pep Guardiola hangover that Enzo Maresca won't be able to remedy.

Meanwhile, Manchester United are never far from a crisis, and despite some apparent stability under Michael Carrick, that won't last much longer.

Arsenal will get in, no problem, and Liverpool's big signings from last season will finally start to shine under the tutelage of Andoni Iraola, with those two teams claiming two spots.

With that, I'm giving my final place to Tottenham Hotspur. That's right; I'm going for the team that finished two points clear of the drop last season.

Business has been good for Spurs in the summer, with the midfield entirely improved, a new center-back who won't find himself suspended every month, and a manager in Roberto de Zerbi who has previously proved adept at Premier League management.

Things are looking good at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, and I'm saying that will lead to a surprising spot in the top four.

Nick Akerman: I think the ordering here is probably the bold bit.

I expect an Andoni Iraola-led Liverpool to finish ahead of Enzo Maresca's Man City. Although much of that relies on Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz remaining fit, the ex-Bournemouth manager is a clear communicator and should get his ideas across quickly to a Reds side that are gasping for new ideas after the malaise of Arne Slot's second year in charge. Maresca will need time to caress Pepisms into his style, despite their similarities.

Leo's excitement for Chelsea does seem worthy of further inspection. Xabi Alonso is an excellent man-manager who can drive underperforming teams to drastic improvement. He has a lot of really good players to work with.

The Spaniard's squad is rammed with options to overcome Man United, Aston Villa and other Champions League contenders who are going through mixed summers. I think they sneak in.

Calum Rogers: I've gone for Liverpool, Manchester City and Manchester United to join Arsenal in the top four, in that order.

I'm a little annoyed Nick has stolen my thunder on Liverpool, but Jérémy Jacquet looks like a strong addition defensively, and the Reds seem likely to make at least one splash signing in attack before the window closes that should aid in rebound seasons for Wirtz and Isak.

City could start slowly as they adjust to a post-Guardiola (and post-Rodri) world, and Maresca may have an impossible job in replacing the six-time Premier League winner. But I can't project a fall out of the top four for a team that has an attack featuring Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Antoine Semenyo, and with more additions looking likely elsewhere.

For the final spot, Chelsea and Tottenham came under consideration, but questions around the futures of Enzo Fernandez and seemingly several others in the squad make it hard to have confidence in the former, while the latter still need to prove that they can make it through a season without their squad being decimated by injuries.

Manchester United have had a quieter summer than both, but the midfield rebuild has been impressive, especially so if they add the physicality of Brighton & Hove Albion's Carlos Baleba to that unit.

The Athletic's David Ornstein has reported they're close to agreeing a deal for the 22-year-old, who would add steel to an exciting collection of technicians in Kobbie Mainoo, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, and that improvement alongside an attack that led the league in goals after manager Michael Carrick took over in January may be enough to cover concerns about a defence that looks short on quality and depth.

Leo Collis: If you saw any of Switzerland's games at the 2026 World Cup, you might have caught a glimpse of Johan Manzambi's show-stealing performances.

He scored twice in an electric 20-minute cameo against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the group stages, and he backed that up with a goal and an assist against Canada from a starting berth.

He then provided an assist against Algeria in the round of 32, before being forced to sit out the rest of the tournament because of injury.

Aston Villa were obviously paying attention, fighting off a number of clubs to secure the 20-year-old's signature. Assuming he can put those injury woes behind him, Manzambi will light up the Premier League just like he did in the tournament in North America.

A change of the guard at Villa Park might be a hindrance, but he showed absolutely no fear of the big stage at his first World Cup, and he'll have no trouble bringing that energy, trickery, and clinical nature to the English top flight.

Nick Akerman: Midfielders are high on everyone's minds this summer. Transfer fees are so inflated that we've gotten to the point where £75 million for Bruno Guimarães seems like insane value, even if he's 28 years old (and I would ask, is 28 even old in modern football?)...

He's the best transfer in the league so far because of how well he fits what Arsenal needs. He's the finished article: a brilliant all-rounder, experienced captain and proven Premier League star.

Mikel Arteta is at the point where he's hunting all trophies, not just trying to land the domestic prize. Bruno is a trinket in a treasure chest already overflowing with gold.

The Brazilian will improve Arsenal in subtle ways. He and Declan Rice should be able to dovetail, interchanging as one bursts forward and the other holds. As we saw in the Community Shield, Bruno is more than capable of running things on his own, which is extremely important during a period in which Rice is juggling persistent injury issues.

In that sense, I can't see any other player being more ready to step in as the former Magpies hero.

Calum Rogers: Brentford smashed their transfer record to sign Mamadou Sangaré from RC Lens, and he looks like a player ready-made for the Premier League and for the Bees.

His energy levels will ensure he's able to handle the league's physicality, but his ability to break up play and quickly start attacks with a keen eye for a pass should pair well with Brentford's counter-attacking style.

Sangaré is not the finished product, but Brentford are the perfect club for him to make an immediate impact while working on his ability to manage and control games in midfield at the highest level.

This summer, we've seen several midfielders sold for fees around the £100 million mark, with elite clubs seemingly laser-focused on physical players like Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes and Elliot Anderson who can do a bit of everything.

Sangaré isn't there yet, but Brentford's exemplary track record in the transfer market is just another indicator that he could be something special.

Live All the Action: Fulham vs. Chelsea 🔥

Leo Collis: Alejandro Garnacho gets away with one because he's only joined Aston Villa on loan, limiting the damage this transfer could do for the west Midlands.

Instead, I'm going for the eye-watering £40 million fee that Leeds United paid Manchester City for James Trafford, a goalkeeper who has never looked as convincing as the hype suggests.

When he was Burnley's No. 1 in the 2023-24 Premier League season, he wasn't comfortable under the high ball and didn't command his penalty box particularly well. Granted, he was only just entering his 20s at the time, but he didn't show much to suggest he would be on the fast-track to becoming a top-flight keeper, and the Clarets plummeted to the Championship.

After sealing a return to Manchester City for 2025-26, he was quickly demoted to the bench when Gianluigi Donnarumma became available. While that deal was difficult to pass up, it showed little confidence in the academy graduate and undoubtedly knocked his confidence.

There's still every chance he can develop into a solid stopper, but that much money for a player who has done little to impress seems like a massive waste of money for Leeds.

Nick Akerman: It was only in December 2025 when Crystal Palace decided to spend £35 million on Tottenham winger Brennan Johnson. Eight months later, he was the make-weight in a swap deal for Everton's Dwight McNeil, which included zero fees.

McNeil is a good player. But that's awful business on the Palace side, who have effectively taken £15 million's worth of a winger who didn't play much last season in exchange for their man who is younger, played at a higher standard, and is worth more.

What transfer strategy is this, other than pulling the ripcord on Johnson, who could have started afresh under Pierre Sage?

Calum Rogers: Newcastle United's summer can kindly be described as risky so far. No one represents that better than midfielder Aladji Bamba, who was signed from AS Monaco for a fee that could rise as high as £34 million, according to Ciaran Kelly of BBC Sport.

For a player who has played just 974 minutes of top-flight football, that is a staggering sum.

There is some promising data behind the Frenchman, who recorded two assists in his limited appearances. As Newcastle pointed out in their reporting of the signing, Bamba was top five in duels won (9.1 per game), tackles (3.6), successful take-ons (1.6) and aerial duels won (1.9) among Ligue 1 midfielders who played more than 500 minutes. And from the eye test, the youngster also clearly possesses the physicality typically required for the Premier League.

However, the small sample size makes those numbers difficult to project forward.

Newcastle have lost key leaders in his position in Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães, focused on signing young players with limited experience to replace them, and hired a coach in Matthias Jaissle with no managerial history in a top European league.

Add it all up, and the chances of Bamba and the other additions making a successful transition to English football look slim.

David Ornstein of The Athletic has credited Newcastle with an interest in 24-year-old Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City, so hopefully the plan is to bring Bamba along slowly.

Even then, though, they have paid a hefty fee for an inexperienced player who faces an uphill battle to make an immediate impact.

Leo Collis: Brentford surprised everyone last season, earning their joint-best Premier League finish despite hiring an unproven manager and losing their starting goalkeeper, captain and two top scorers ahead of the campaign.

The Bees will get found out this time around, with teams being more wary of the threat posed by the potent but limited Igor Thiago and crowding out the big Brazilian's route to goal.

Sunderland will suffer a similar fate. Another surprise team in 2025-26, the Black Cats finished a remarkable seventh after earning promotion to the top flight from the Championship playoffs the season before.

That success could come back to haunt Regis Le Bris' side, as it will now have to deal with European football on top of another bruising Premier League campaign. With little investment in the squad so far this summer, there isn't enough quality to earn good results across both competitions, and their league form might suffer.

Finally, Hull City will have to be careful that their return to the top tier of English football doesn't end in humiliation. The Tigers' promotion was surprising in the first place, and despite the success of the promoted clubs last season, a lack of quality signings and a poor base to start with will condemn the Yorkshire side to a quick return to the Championship.

Nick Akerman: My picks mean Frank Lampard will keep Coventry City in the Premier League. I think it'll be close, but there's a good chance Fulham will become the next high-profile London side to follow West Ham into the Championship.

The Cottagers need to quickly adjust to life without Marco Silva. His management kept them safe during moments when they didn't look particularly great last season. New boss Álvaro Arbeloa made Real Madrid worse during his stint, and I think we'll see that on a larger scale here, given that Fulham isn't one of the best teams in the division, unlike Los Blancos in Spain.

Hull and Ipswich, I'm sorry. I just can't see them overcoming the mid-to-bottom pack, especially if the division plays out as brutally as it did last year.

Calum Rogers: I agree with Leo and Nick that Sunderland and Fulham are in danger, but remember earlier when I said I'm a coward? Well, I'm picking Hull, Coventry and Ipswich to get relegated.

But after a season that saw two promoted teams comfortably stay up and even qualify for Europe in Sunderland's case, maybe that's actually the boldest prediction someone could make? No? Well, I'm doing it anyway.

All three of the newbies have been busy, but it's just not enough...yet.

Hull have signed 11 players, but with the average age of those additions hovering around 22 years old, it's questionable whether they have added enough experience to truly make a go of surviving.

Coventry and Ipswich have brought in a decent mix of youth and experience.

The Sky Blues have added Gus Hamer and Taiwo Awoniyi, who have each previously recorded 10 goal contributions in a Premier League season, while the Tractor Boys' Julio Enciso and Abdul Fatawu are exciting young attackers who have shown glimpses of being able to have an impact in the division.

A couple of impact signings could still turn the tide, but I'm sticking with the promoted trio as my relegation picks for now.

Leo Collis: Pep Guardiola has left big shoes to fill at Manchester City. The Catalan won pretty much everything available to him during a decade at the Etihad Stadium, and despite the clear spending capital available, he was still pivotal in molding the squad into an all-conquering juggernaut.

Enzo Maresca comes in with a relatively light CV. He had just a season-and-a-half at Chelsea before his controversial departure, earning a fourth-place Premier League finish in his first season and then leaving Stamford Bridge with the club just fifth in the English top flight. A Conference League title and a Club World Cup look good in the trophy cabinet, but they are minor trophies in the grand scheme of things.

With Manchester City, he'll struggle to impose himself on a squad that only just said goodbye to the influential Guardiola, and the results will suffer. The talent is clearly still available—although the imminent departure of Rodri is a huge loss—but the 46-year-old won't be able to accentuate their abilities as his mentor could.

Consequently, City will slip out of title contention, won't make the top four, and could even struggle to finish in the top six.

Nick Akerman: Michael Carrick pretty much backed Man United into a corner after his excellent stint as interim boss led them to a Champions League place.

It would have been bold for the board to hire someone else full-time, just in case the alternative failed and accusations that Carrick never received his opportunity came their way.

While Carrick's extended tenure was a given, few supporters will be happy with how he's being backed in the transfer market. We're one week away from United's first match of the season, and Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans are the club's big midfield signings (with Carlos Baleba likely to come soon). Good deals if taken at face value, but not enough.

Where's the next left back? Where's the competition for Benjamin Sesko up front? How is United seriously on the verge of lining up with the same creaking defense they had in 2022?

Carrick showed signs of tactical naivety at times, but was bailed out by players in great form. He is now under much greater pressure. I think it could go wrong at speed, hastened by a twitchy INEOS who may be quick to move on if the new boss turns out to be another pretender.

Calum Rogers: Jeez, an awful lot of negativity here, guys. Haven't you heard that preseason is the time when every team has hope?

I guess it's on me to send the readers off with a feel-good prediction, so here goes nothing: Brentford will finish in the top six.

How you feel about this likely comes down to your take on Brentford winning just one of their final 10 games last season, tumbling from as high as fifth in January to a ninth-place finish and missing out on European qualification on goal difference.

Did the league figure them out? Or did a thin squad just run out of steam and a bit of luck?

Clearly, I'm going with the latter, and Brentford's summer business looks to have addressed the depth problem. Callum Wilson and Jaidon Anthony provide options for rotation and can change games off the bench, while I've already explained how excited I am about Sangaré in midfield.

With so much upheaval at the top end of the table, and with other usual top-six challengers like Aston Villa and Newcastle also losing significant players, there's another opportunity for a smaller club to follow in Bournemouth's footsteps from last season, and Brentford look the most likely to me.

Leo Collis: It's clear I haven't learned my lesson from last season , when I picked Chelsea to win the title off the back of a convincing Club World Cup win.

There has been no such silverware heading into the 2026-27 campaign, and the Blues are coming off a season in which they finished a distant 10th in the Premier League. That makes this pick even more ludicrous.

But with new manager Xabi Alonso in the dugout, things feel quite hopeful. Meanwhile, some shrewd signings, including the excellent Morgan Rogers, in addition to some much-needed experience in the dressing room courtesy of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, should change the atmosphere at Stamford Bridge for the better.

With European football off the calendar, the Blues can focus their attention on a strong domestic campaign. With Arsenal perhaps prioritizing a first European Cup title in club history, that could play nicely into Chelsea's hands.

Honestly, Arsenal should be going back-to-back. But we're in the business of bold, and much like last season, bold is blue.

Nick Akerman: I swear I'm not doing this on purpose. I realize picking Arsenal to win the title right now is like saying night will turn to day.

Mikel Arteta's squad are by far the deepest and best-prepped in the Premier League. Defending the crown is non-negotiable, and to be honest, success should be measured by whether or not the Gunners finally win the Champions League, because the rest of the English clubs are just not in a position to compete with them.

So, to get bold with it, I think there's a genuine chance Arsenal could win the title with the highest-ever gap to second place.

Manchester City's 2017-18 Centurions currently hold the record, finishing 19 points ahead of rivals Manchester United. Arteta's side won't reach 100 points, but their nearest rivals are all dealing with issues that may lead to inconsistency. Let's go with a 20-point title win for the North Londoners.

Calum Rogers: Arsenal have made upgrades to a title-winning team. Christos Tzolis looks to have added more juice to the team's attack, while the addition of Bruno Guimarães affords manager Mikel Arteta more options both tactically and in terms of rotation.

The Athletic's David Ornstein, Jacob Tanswell and James McNicholas have also reported that Arsenal have agreed a deal for Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa, which would add to an already deep defensive unit. The 28-year-old England international will also help cover for the injured William Saliba, who will be out until around October with a back injury.

There are still concerns in attack, namely over the fitness of Bukayo Saka and whether Viktor Gyökeres can offer a more consistent threat, and perhaps there will be a lull after the emotionally draining chase for a first league title since 2004. While I still think Arsenal have enough to repeat, my somewhat spicy take is that they will do so with fewer points than the 85 they recorded last season.

He then provided an assist against Algeria in the round of 32, before being forced to sit out the rest of the tournament because of injury.

Aston Villa were obviously paying attention, fighting off a number of clubs to secure the 20-year-old's signature. Assuming he can put those injury woes behind him, Manzambi will light up the Premier League just like he did in the tournament in North America.

A change of the guard at Villa Park might be a hindrance, but he showed absolutely no fear of the big stage at his first World Cup, and he'll have no trouble bringing that energy, trickery, and clinical nature to the English top flight.

Nick Akerman: Midfielders are high on everyone's minds this summer. Transfer fees are so inflated that we've gotten to the point where £75 million for Bruno Guimarães seems like insane value, even if he's 28 years old (and I would ask, is 28 even old in modern football?)...
He's the best transfer in the league so far because of how well he fits what Arsenal needs. He's the finished article: a brilliant all-rounder, experienced captain and proven Premier League star.
Mikel Arteta is at the point where he's hunting all trophies, not just trying to land the domestic prize. Bruno is a trinket in a treasure chest already overflowing with gold.

The Brazilian will improve Arsenal in subtle ways. He and Declan Rice should be able to dovetail, interchanging as one bursts forward and the other holds. As we saw in the Community Shield, Bruno is more than capable of running things on his own, which is extremely important during a period in which Rice is juggling persistent injury issues.
In that sense, I can't see any other player being more ready to step in as the former Magpies hero.
Calum Rogers: Brentford smashed their transfer record to sign Mamadou Sangaré from RC Lens, and he looks like a player ready-made for the Premier League and for the Bees.

His energy levels will ensure he's able to handle the league's physicality, but his ability to break up play and quickly start attacks with a keen eye for a pass should pair well with Brentford's counter-attacking style.
Sangaré is not the finished product, but Brentford are the perfect club for him to make an immediate impact while working on his ability to manage and control games in midfield at the highest level.

This summer, we've seen several midfielders sold for fees around the £100 million mark, with elite clubs seemingly laser-focused on physical players like Sandro Tonali, Mateus Fernandes and Elliot Anderson who can do a bit of everything.
Sangaré isn't there yet, but Brentford's exemplary track record in the transfer market is just another indicator that he could be something special.
Live All the Action: Fulham vs. Chelsea 🔥
Leo Collis: Alejandro Garnacho gets away with one because he's only joined Aston Villa on loan, limiting the damage this transfer could do for the west Midlands.
Instead, I'm going for the eye-watering £40 million fee that Leeds United paid Manchester City for James Trafford, a goalkeeper who has never looked as convincing as the hype suggests.

When he was Burnley's No. 1 in the 2023-24 Premier League season, he wasn't comfortable under the high ball and didn't command his penalty box particularly well. Granted, he was only just entering his 20s at the time, but he didn't show much to suggest he would be on the fast-track to becoming a top-flight keeper, and the Clarets plummeted to the Championship.

After sealing a return to Manchester City for 2025-26, he was quickly demoted to the bench when Gianluigi Donnarumma became available. While that deal was difficult to pass up, it showed little confidence in the academy graduate and undoubtedly knocked his confidence.
There's still every chance he can develop into a solid stopper, but that much money for a player who has done little to impress seems like a massive waste of money for Leeds.

Nick Akerman: It was only in December 2025 when Crystal Palace decided to spend £35 million on Tottenham winger Brennan Johnson. Eight months later, he was the make-weight in a swap deal for Everton's Dwight McNeil, which included zero fees.

McNeil is a good player. But that's awful business on the Palace side, who have effectively taken £15 million's worth of a winger who didn't play much last season in exchange for their man who is younger, played at a higher standard, and is worth more.
What transfer strategy is this, other than pulling the ripcord on Johnson, who could have started afresh under Pierre Sage?

Calum Rogers: Newcastle United's summer can kindly be described as risky so far. No one represents that better than midfielder Aladji Bamba, who was signed from AS Monaco for a fee that could rise as high as £34 million, according to Ciaran Kelly of BBC Sport.
For a player who has played just 974 minutes of top-flight football, that is a staggering sum.

There is some promising data behind the Frenchman, who recorded two assists in his limited appearances. As Newcastle pointed out in their reporting of the signing, Bamba was top five in duels won (9.1 per game), tackles (3.6), successful take-ons (1.6) and aerial duels won (1.9) among Ligue 1 midfielders who played more than 500 minutes. And from the eye test, the youngster also clearly possesses the physicality typically required for the Premier League.
However, the small sample size makes those numbers difficult to project forward.

Newcastle have lost key leaders in his position in Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães, focused on signing young players with limited experience to replace them, and hired a coach in Matthias Jaissle with no managerial history in a top European league.
Add it all up, and the chances of Bamba and the other additions making a successful transition to English football look slim.
David Ornstein of The Athletic has credited Newcastle with an interest in 24-year-old Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City, so hopefully the plan is to bring Bamba along slowly.
Even then, though, they have paid a hefty fee for an inexperienced player who faces an uphill battle to make an immediate impact.

Leo Collis: Brentford surprised everyone last season, earning their joint-best Premier League finish despite hiring an unproven manager and losing their starting goalkeeper, captain and two top scorers ahead of the campaign.
The Bees will get found out this time around, with teams being more wary of the threat posed by the potent but limited Igor Thiago and crowding out the big Brazilian's route to goal.

Sunderland will suffer a similar fate. Another surprise team in 2025-26, the Black Cats finished a remarkable seventh after earning promotion to the top flight from the Championship playoffs the season before.

That success could come back to haunt Regis Le Bris' side, as it will now have to deal with European football on top of another bruising Premier League campaign. With little investment in the squad so far this summer, there isn't enough quality to earn good results across both competitions, and their league form might suffer.

Finally, Hull City will have to be careful that their return to the top tier of English football doesn't end in humiliation. The Tigers' promotion was surprising in the first place, and despite the success of the promoted clubs last season, a lack of quality signings and a poor base to start with will condemn the Yorkshire side to a quick return to the Championship.

Nick Akerman: My picks mean Frank Lampard will keep Coventry City in the Premier League. I think it'll be close, but there's a good chance Fulham will become the next high-profile London side to follow West Ham into the Championship.

The Cottagers need to quickly adjust to life without Marco Silva. His management kept them safe during moments when they didn't look particularly great last season. New boss Álvaro Arbeloa made Real Madrid worse during his stint, and I think we'll see that on a larger scale here, given that Fulham isn't one of the best teams in the division, unlike Los Blancos in Spain.
Hull and Ipswich, I'm sorry. I just can't see them overcoming the mid-to-bottom pack, especially if the division plays out as brutally as it did last year.
Calum Rogers: I agree with Leo and Nick that Sunderland and Fulham are in danger, but remember earlier when I said I'm a coward? Well, I'm picking Hull, Coventry and Ipswich to get relegated.

But after a season that saw two promoted teams comfortably stay up and even qualify for Europe in Sunderland's case, maybe that's actually the boldest prediction someone could make? No? Well, I'm doing it anyway.
All three of the newbies have been busy, but it's just not enough...yet.
Hull have signed 11 players, but with the average age of those additions hovering around 22 years old, it's questionable whether they have added enough experience to truly make a go of surviving.
Coventry and Ipswich have brought in a decent mix of youth and experience.

The Sky Blues have added Gus Hamer and Taiwo Awoniyi, who have each previously recorded 10 goal contributions in a Premier League season, while the Tractor Boys' Julio Enciso and Abdul Fatawu are exciting young attackers who have shown glimpses of being able to have an impact in the division.
A couple of impact signings could still turn the tide, but I'm sticking with the promoted trio as my relegation picks for now.

Leo Collis: Pep Guardiola has left big shoes to fill at Manchester City. The Catalan won pretty much everything available to him during a decade at the Etihad Stadium, and despite the clear spending capital available, he was still pivotal in molding the squad into an all-conquering juggernaut.

Enzo Maresca comes in with a relatively light CV. He had just a season-and-a-half at Chelsea before his controversial departure, earning a fourth-place Premier League finish in his first season and then leaving Stamford Bridge with the club just fifth in the English top flight. A Conference League title and a Club World Cup look good in the trophy cabinet, but they are minor trophies in the grand scheme of things.

With Manchester City, he'll struggle to impose himself on a squad that only just said goodbye to the influential Guardiola, and the results will suffer. The talent is clearly still available—although the imminent departure of Rodri is a huge loss—but the 46-year-old won't be able to accentuate their abilities as his mentor could.
Consequently, City will slip out of title contention, won't make the top four, and could even struggle to finish in the top six.
Nick Akerman: Michael Carrick pretty much backed Man United into a corner after his excellent stint as interim boss led them to a Champions League place.
It would have been bold for the board to hire someone else full-time, just in case the alternative failed and accusations that Carrick never received his opportunity came their way.

While Carrick's extended tenure was a given, few supporters will be happy with how he's being backed in the transfer market. We're one week away from United's first match of the season, and Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans are the club's big midfield signings (with Carlos Baleba likely to come soon). Good deals if taken at face value, but not enough.
Where's the next left back? Where's the competition for Benjamin Sesko up front? How is United seriously on the verge of lining up with the same creaking defense they had in 2022?

Carrick showed signs of tactical naivety at times, but was bailed out by players in great form. He is now under much greater pressure. I think it could go wrong at speed, hastened by a twitchy INEOS who may be quick to move on if the new boss turns out to be another pretender.
Calum Rogers: Jeez, an awful lot of negativity here, guys. Haven't you heard that preseason is the time when every team has hope?
I guess it's on me to send the readers off with a feel-good prediction, so here goes nothing: Brentford will finish in the top six.

How you feel about this likely comes down to your take on Brentford winning just one of their final 10 games last season, tumbling from as high as fifth in January to a ninth-place finish and missing out on European qualification on goal difference.
Did the league figure them out? Or did a thin squad just run out of steam and a bit of luck?

Clearly, I'm going with the latter, and Brentford's summer business looks to have addressed the depth problem. Callum Wilson and Jaidon Anthony provide options for rotation and can change games off the bench, while I've already explained how excited I am about Sangaré in midfield.

With so much upheaval at the top end of the table, and with other usual top-six challengers like Aston Villa and Newcastle also losing significant players, there's another opportunity for a smaller club to follow in Bournemouth's footsteps from last season, and Brentford look the most likely to me.
Leo Collis: It's clear I haven't learned my lesson from last season , when I picked Chelsea to win the title off the back of a convincing Club World Cup win.

There has been no such silverware heading into the 2026-27 campaign, and the Blues are coming off a season in which they finished a distant 10th in the Premier League. That makes this pick even more ludicrous.

But with new manager Xabi Alonso in the dugout, things feel quite hopeful. Meanwhile, some shrewd signings, including the excellent Morgan Rogers, in addition to some much-needed experience in the dressing room courtesy of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, should change the atmosphere at Stamford Bridge for the better.

With European football off the calendar, the Blues can focus their attention on a strong domestic campaign. With Arsenal perhaps prioritizing a first European Cup title in club history, that could play nicely into Chelsea's hands.
Honestly, Arsenal should be going back-to-back. But we're in the business of bold, and much like last season, bold is blue.
Nick Akerman: I swear I'm not doing this on purpose. I realize picking Arsenal to win the title right now is like saying night will turn to day.

Mikel Arteta's squad are by far the deepest and best-prepped in the Premier League. Defending the crown is non-negotiable, and to be honest, success should be measured by whether or not the Gunners finally win the Champions League, because the rest of the English clubs are just not in a position to compete with them.
So, to get bold with it, I think there's a genuine chance Arsenal could win the title with the highest-ever gap to second place.

Manchester City's 2017-18 Centurions currently hold the record, finishing 19 points ahead of rivals Manchester United. Arteta's side won't reach 100 points, but their nearest rivals are all dealing with issues that may lead to inconsistency. Let's go with a 20-point title win for the North Londoners.

Calum Rogers: Arsenal have made upgrades to a title-winning team. Christos Tzolis looks to have added more juice to the team's attack, while the addition of Bruno Guimarães affords manager Mikel Arteta more options both tactically and in terms of rotation.

The Athletic's David Ornstein, Jacob Tanswell and James McNicholas have also reported that Arsenal have agreed a deal for Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa, which would add to an already deep defensive unit. The 28-year-old England international will also help cover for the injured William Saliba, who will be out until around October with a back injury.

There are still concerns in attack, namely over the fitness of Bukayo Saka and whether Viktor Gyökeres can offer a more consistent threat, and perhaps there will be a lull after the emotionally draining chase for a first league title since 2004. While I still think Arsenal have enough to repeat, my somewhat spicy take is that they will do so with fewer points than the 85 they recorded last season.

articles.title: Cuestión de liderazgo
articles.standfirst: Flick quiere a Rodri por su fútbol, pero también para que sea un de los jefes del equipo
articles.summary: Flick quiere a Rodri por su fútbol, pero también para que sea un de los jefes del equipo
articles.body: La llegada de Rodrigo Hernández supone un cambio de paradigma en el presente azulgrana. El ex del Manchester City, campeón de todos los títulos posibles con el conjunto británico y de Mundial, Eurocopa y Nations League con la selección española, ha aterrizado en el vestuario del Barça con los galones suficientes para ser el líder que guíe a los jóvenes de la plantilla a conquistar, de nuevo, la ansiada Champions League y mantener la hegemonía a nivel nacional. La salida de Robert Lewandowski tras unos años de liderazgo en el vestuario, supuso perder un referente en los grandes partidos. El polaco, tirando de veteranía, era el que muchas ocasiones ponía calma y aconsejaba a los jugadores jóvenes en momentos donde algo fallaba o el nerviosismo se apoderaba. Además, en este mercado también ha salido Ronald Araujo dirección Liverpool. El uruguayo, con menos protagonismo en el césped, ejercía de hermano mayor para muchos chicos y era una de las personas más queridas dentro del vestuario, además de ser uno de los portadores del brazalete de capitán. Si a esto le sumamos la marcha de Ter Stegen, en el cuerpo técnico tenían claro que necesitaban a un jerarca al lado de Raphinha, a una persona que orientara al equipo dentro y, sobre todo, fuera del terreno de juego. Lo que sale de la Ciudad Deportiva Joan Gamper horas después de la llegada de Rodri es un mensaje claro: “Hemos fichado a un líder”. Y eso es lo que quería, y por lo que ha luchado, un Fick que respira con esta incorporación. Tener un capitán, en principio, sin brazalete. La reestructuración en la capitanía es total. La temporada pasada los capitanes eran Ter Stegen, Araujo, De Jong, Raphinha y Pedri. Dos de estos cinco están fuera del club y Hansi Flick ha decidido quitarle ese poder provisional al neerlandés hasta que vuelva de lesión o se hagan las votaciones finales cuando la plantilla esté cerrada. "Hasta que eso suceda, Raphinha será el capitán, junto a Eric y Gavi", comentó el germano en declaraciones al club.  Con el ascenso de Raphinha a primer capitán y la incorporación de Eric y Gavi, se hace difícil pensar que Rodri pueda optar a portar el brazalete, aunque la última palabra la tendrán unos futbolistas que ven al centrocampista madrileño como un referente.

articles.title: B/R's Guide to Picking a Premier League Team for Casual Soccer Fans
articles.summary: Soccer has historically been a hard sell for American sports fans. At least, that was the case until the 2026 FIFA World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, which gave everyone football fever for just over a month. (Yes, it's called football. Deal with it.)
articles.body:
Soccer has historically been a hard sell for American sports fans. At least, that was the case until the 2026 FIFA World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, which gave everyone football fever for just over a month. (Yes, it's called football. Deal with it.)

While the World Cup is over after Spain's 1-0 victory over Lionel Messi and Argentina in the final, the European football season is just about to get started.

England's Premier League is perhaps the most successful, most exciting club division on the planet. Americans who are looking to get their football fix outside of Major League Soccer should turn their gaze across the Atlantic.

But with 20 teams to choose from, which is the best option?

Here, we've looked at every club in the 2026-27 Premier League season and outlined the reasons why they might be worth following (or not).

Arsenal are the reigning Premier League champions and the favorites to win it again in 2026-27. If glory is what you're looking for, the Gunners are your best shot.

Boasting the finest squad depth in the division, one of the world's best midfielders in Declan Rice and a near-impenetrable defense, Arsenal are well-equipped to dominate English football for the next half-decade.

You might have to sit through a few more 1-0 wins than you would with other Premier League sides (they had eight in 2025-26), but it doesn't matter as long as the three points are earned.

The so-called Premier League "Big Six" might not be a thing anymore. But if any club were to push that number to seven, Aston Villa would be it.

The Villans (not a typo) finished fourth last season and won the UEFA Europa League. Manager Unai Emery has proved himself a master of European competitions, and he's made his team a tough opponent domestically.

If you needed any further convincing, stamps of approval don't come much better than from the British royal family. Prince William, heir to the throne, regularly turns up at Villa Park to cheer on the team in the most awkward way imaginable .

The West Midlanders have had to adapt after losing a handful of key players, but they've strengthened well and should again be considered dark horses for a title push.

If You Love a Plucky Underdog: Bournemouth

Bournemouth, lovingly known as the Cherries, are from a seaside town on England's south coast. Their home ground, the Vitality Stadium, has the lowest capacity among the current crop of Premier League sides.

In their last four seasons in the English top flight, Bournemouth have had to compete with teams with significantly larger budgets to spend on talent. Still, through excellent recruitment and an admirable attacking philosophy, the club has performed well above expectations.

You might not want to get too attached to the players, since bigger clubs often pluck them away. But you can watch the progression of those talents and flaunt your knowledge of them when they step up to the big time.

Live All the Action: Fulham vs. Chelsea 🔥

One for the environmentalists here. If you have an affinity for bees and understand the importance of protecting them , supporting a team with a winged pollinator as its mascot is a great option.

Just like their fuzzy insect talisman, Brentford are having an outsized impact on a wider ecosystem. Despite playing in one of the division's smallest stadiums and operating on one of the tightest budgets, the Bees reached a remarkable ninth in the Premier League last season, coming within inches of a place in European competition.

Brentford also have a self-described "no d--kheads" transfer policy , and two of their players came to the aid of a man who was subjected to racist abuse earlier this year.

Brentford are an impossibly likable club, so you won't even get a lot of grief from rival fans.

If You Want to Discover Up-and-Coming Talent: Brighton & Hove Albion

The talent factory at Brighton & Hove Albion is the envy of many Premier League sides.

The Seagulls have a habit of signing rising stars, developing them into top-quality players and selling them on for a hefty profit.

Players such as Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool and Argentina), Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid and Spain), Moisés Caicedo (Chelsea and Ecuador) and João Pedro (Chelsea and Brazil) have all passed through the Amex Stadium on the way to bigger things.

Of course, that makes Brighton a highly competitive team, picking up fine results against the league's big guns with regularity.

If finding the next big thing in football sounds like the best way to enjoy the game, Brighton are the way to go.

While the hatred for certain Premier League clubs among fans can wax and wane depending on success, managerial appointments or players, the vitriol for Chelsea is reasonably consistent.

Part of that stems from the fact that the Blues effectively heralded the era of billionaire owners using English clubs as playthings.

Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich bought the club in 2003 and proceeded to spend heavily on star players. That started a period of dominance that brought a bucketload of major trophies over the next decade and a half.

While other clubs have taken a similar pathway in the ensuing years, the collective annoyance towards the West Londoners persists, even if it's not quite as strong as it once was.

Now, under Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Clearlake Capital, the club is mocked for its scattergun spending that hasn't delivered much tangible success.

If you love playing a villain or enjoy being a source of irritation, put on a Chelsea shirt.

If You Love a Good Comeback Story: Coventry City

Coventry City are back in the Premier League for the first time since the 2000-01 season. The Sky Blues took a long and winding road to get back in.

Amid financial difficulties and a poor ownership structure, they slipped to the fourth tier of English football (League Two) following the 2016-17 campaign. All that turmoil came while they didn't have a secure home ground.

The Coventry Building Society Arena had been built for the Sky Blues, but because of complicated ownership agreements over the stadium, they were often forced to play elsewhere. According to BBC News , they played at four "home" grounds after leaving th eir previous stadium, Highfield Road, in 2005.

But the CBS Arena has finally been brought under club ownership, and the future looks bright for the West Midlands club.

If a redemption arc is what you're looking for from your chosen team, they don't come much better than Coventry City's.

If You're a Philadelphia Eagles Fan: Crystal Palace

For Philadelphia Eagles fans looking for their round-ball team, Crystal Palace should be on your radar. Both teams have an eagle as their mascot, but the connection runs deeper than that.

Over the years, eagles named Challenger and Lincoln have flown around Lincoln Financial Field on game days. Each bird has also been present for Palace's pre-season tour events in the United States.

While the Philadelphia Eagles have Swoop , who rallies the crowd during home games, Palace have Pete and Alice . The South Londoners are also training a bald eagle, Phoenix , to be their next live mascot, replacing Kayla, who died in 2020.

Selhurst Park would feel like a home away from home for Eagles fans, and it also served as the filming location for stadium scenes in Ted Lasso .

While many sports fans will be familiar with Liverpool, they may be less aware of their Merseyside neighbors.

Everton have actually been around longer than their local rivals, founded in 1878. By contrast, Liverpool were only formed in 1892.

Historically, though, the younger side have had more success, with Liverpool winning 20 top-flight titles compared to Everton's nine.

The club's home grounds used to be less than a mile apart, but since the Blues moved to Hill Dickinson Stadium before the 2025-26 season, that distance has extended to over two miles. That hasn't made the rivalry any less heated, though.

The pair of matches between the sides in a Premier League season, known as Merseyside derbies, are always appointment viewing. Everton love nothing more than depriving their neighbors of valuable points.

If you love to get the upper hand on the folks next door, Everton will suit you nicely.

Connections between professional wrestling and football aren't difficult to find.

Former WWE star Sheamus is a huge Liverpool fan , while Drew McIntyre isn't shy about his love of Scottish side Rangers.

Premier League legend Wayne Rooney famously slapped Wade Barrett at a WWE Raw recording in November 2015, while Declan Rice and Mason Mount were filmed imitating Edge at an England training camp in 2021.

But All Elite Wrestling has the most significant presence in the Premier League as it stands. Company president Tony Khan serves as the vice-chairman and director of football operations for Fulham. In fact, AEW is the shirt sponsor for the Fulham women's team.

For those who have pledged their allegiance to the upstart wrestling promotion, the West Londoners are the logical choice when picking a football team to follow.

If You're Not Scared of the Drop: Hull City

Hull City have returned to the Premier League for the first time since the 2016-17 season, earning promotion following a dramatic victory in the Championship playoff final.

However, the Tigers have never stuck around for more than two seasons in their previous trips to the top flight, and their last visit lasted only one.

If you like living on the edge and aren't scared of the prospect of your team dropping down to a lower division, the Yorkshire side could be worth a follow.

You're likely to see a lot of goals scored in Hull's matches; they just might not be coming from the team wearing amber and black.

That headline alone might have already cost us most of you. However, Ipswich Town are the team of the ginger song-machine's heart, and he's even a minority stakeholder in the club.

After the team's promotion to the Premier League in May, he was filmed giving an, erm, delightful rendition of his hit song "The A-Team" in the dressing room, along with the squad.

Sheeran's Mathematics Tour logo even donned the club's shirts for the last four seasons, although a new sponsor will be in place for 2026-27 and beyond.

So if you're a fan of the " Shape of You " singer, Ipswich could be a " Perfect " fit.

49ers Enterprises, the investment arm behind the San Francisco 49ers, took full ownership of Leeds United in 2023. That was the same year that the Niners lost the Super Bowl final to the Kansas City Chiefs, so read into that what you will.

Bad omens aside, Leeds successfully stayed in the Premier League last season after rising up from the league below, finishing in a comfortable 14th position.

The club is steadily building on that success with a handful of smart signings. A push into the top half of the table wouldn't be out of the question this time around.

Leeds actually won the last English top-flight title before the division was rebranded as the Premier League in 1992. While another trophy might be a while away yet, the club is clearly on an upward trajectory.

According to a 2025-26 Men in Blazers survey , Liverpool was named the top supported Premier League team among U.S. fans, picking up a hefty 22 percent share.

The club already has plenty of U.S. connections, with owners Fenway Sports Group also having the Boston Red Sox and NASCAR's RFK Racing under its umbrella.

But perhaps the most notable link is NBA legend LeBron James, who owns a stake in the team. The Philadelphia 76ers star is regularly seen donning Liverpool shirts and other merchandise, and he even launched a collaborative fashion collection with the club in 2023.

For fans of The King, rooting for Liverpool is an easy decision.

If You Love Robot Goal Machines: Manchester City

If you were among the many Americans captivated by the 2026 World Cup, one particular Norwegian likely grabbed your attention.

Erling Haaland didn't just win over fans for his embracing of U.S. culture or his fantastic choice in souvenirs . He also scored a ton of goals.

Despite exiting at the quarter-final stage, Haaland managed to find the net seven times in just five games, including a pair of strikes in a 2-1 victory over Brazil in the round of 32.

paragraphs: Soccer has historically been a hard sell for American sports fans. At least, that was the case until the 2026 FIFA World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, which gave everyone football fever for just over a month. (Yes, it's called football. Deal with it.)
While the World Cup is over after Spain's 1-0 victory over Lionel Messi and Argentina in the final, the European football season is just about to get started.

England's Premier League is perhaps the most successful, most exciting club division on the planet. Americans who are looking to get their football fix outside of Major League Soccer should turn their gaze across the Atlantic.
But with 20 teams to choose from, which is the best option?
Here, we've looked at every club in the 2026-27 Premier League season and outlined the reasons why they might be worth following (or not).
Arsenal are the reigning Premier League champions and the favorites to win it again in 2026-27. If glory is what you're looking for, the Gunners are your best shot.

Boasting the finest squad depth in the division, one of the world's best midfielders in Declan Rice and a near-impenetrable defense, Arsenal are well-equipped to dominate English football for the next half-decade.
You might have to sit through a few more 1-0 wins than you would with other Premier League sides (they had eight in 2025-26), but it doesn't matter as long as the three points are earned.
The so-called Premier League "Big Six" might not be a thing anymore. But if any club were to push that number to seven, Aston Villa would be it.

The Villans (not a typo) finished fourth last season and won the UEFA Europa League. Manager Unai Emery has proved himself a master of European competitions, and he's made his team a tough opponent domestically.

If you needed any further convincing, stamps of approval don't come much better than from the British royal family. Prince William, heir to the throne, regularly turns up at Villa Park to cheer on the team in the most awkward way imaginable .
The West Midlanders have had to adapt after losing a handful of key players, but they've strengthened well and should again be considered dark horses for a title push.
If You Love a Plucky Underdog: Bournemouth

Bournemouth, lovingly known as the Cherries, are from a seaside town on England's south coast. Their home ground, the Vitality Stadium, has the lowest capacity among the current crop of Premier League sides.

In their last four seasons in the English top flight, Bournemouth have had to compete with teams with significantly larger budgets to spend on talent. Still, through excellent recruitment and an admirable attacking philosophy, the club has performed well above expectations.

You might not want to get too attached to the players, since bigger clubs often pluck them away. But you can watch the progression of those talents and flaunt your knowledge of them when they step up to the big time.
Live All the Action: Fulham vs. Chelsea 🔥
One for the environmentalists here. If you have an affinity for bees and understand the importance of protecting them , supporting a team with a winged pollinator as its mascot is a great option.

Just like their fuzzy insect talisman, Brentford are having an outsized impact on a wider ecosystem. Despite playing in one of the division's smallest stadiums and operating on one of the tightest budgets, the Bees reached a remarkable ninth in the Premier League last season, coming within inches of a place in European competition.
Brentford also have a self-described "no d--kheads" transfer policy , and two of their players came to the aid of a man who was subjected to racist abuse earlier this year.
Brentford are an impossibly likable club, so you won't even get a lot of grief from rival fans.
If You Want to Discover Up-and-Coming Talent: Brighton & Hove Albion
The talent factory at Brighton & Hove Albion is the envy of many Premier League sides.
The Seagulls have a habit of signing rising stars, developing them into top-quality players and selling them on for a hefty profit.

Players such as Alexis Mac Allister (Liverpool and Argentina), Marc Cucurella (Real Madrid and Spain), Moisés Caicedo (Chelsea and Ecuador) and João Pedro (Chelsea and Brazil) have all passed through the Amex Stadium on the way to bigger things.
Of course, that makes Brighton a highly competitive team, picking up fine results against the league's big guns with regularity.
If finding the next big thing in football sounds like the best way to enjoy the game, Brighton are the way to go.
While the hatred for certain Premier League clubs among fans can wax and wane depending on success, managerial appointments or players, the vitriol for Chelsea is reasonably consistent.
Part of that stems from the fact that the Blues effectively heralded the era of billionaire owners using English clubs as playthings.

Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich bought the club in 2003 and proceeded to spend heavily on star players. That started a period of dominance that brought a bucketload of major trophies over the next decade and a half.
While other clubs have taken a similar pathway in the ensuing years, the collective annoyance towards the West Londoners persists, even if it's not quite as strong as it once was.
Now, under Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Clearlake Capital, the club is mocked for its scattergun spending that hasn't delivered much tangible success.
If you love playing a villain or enjoy being a source of irritation, put on a Chelsea shirt.

Coventry City are back in the Premier League for the first time since the 2000-01 season. The Sky Blues took a long and winding road to get back in.

Amid financial difficulties and a poor ownership structure, they slipped to the fourth tier of English football (League Two) following the 2016-17 campaign. All that turmoil came while they didn't have a secure home ground.

The Coventry Building Society Arena had been built for the Sky Blues, but because of complicated ownership agreements over the stadium, they were often forced to play elsewhere. According to BBC News , they played at four "home" grounds after leaving th eir previous stadium, Highfield Road, in 2005.
But the CBS Arena has finally been brought under club ownership, and the future looks bright for the West Midlands club.
If a redemption arc is what you're looking for from your chosen team, they don't come much better than Coventry City's.

For Philadelphia Eagles fans looking for their round-ball team, Crystal Palace should be on your radar. Both teams have an eagle as their mascot, but the connection runs deeper than that.
Over the years, eagles named Challenger and Lincoln have flown around Lincoln Financial Field on game days. Each bird has also been present for Palace's pre-season tour events in the United States.

While the Philadelphia Eagles have Swoop , who rallies the crowd during home games, Palace have Pete and Alice . The South Londoners are also training a bald eagle, Phoenix , to be their next live mascot, replacing Kayla, who died in 2020.
Selhurst Park would feel like a home away from home for Eagles fans, and it also served as the filming location for stadium scenes in Ted Lasso .
While many sports fans will be familiar with Liverpool, they may be less aware of their Merseyside neighbors.
Everton have actually been around longer than their local rivals, founded in 1878. By contrast, Liverpool were only formed in 1892.
Historically, though, the younger side have had more success, with Liverpool winning 20 top-flight titles compared to Everton's nine.

The club's home grounds used to be less than a mile apart, but since the Blues moved to Hill Dickinson Stadium before the 2025-26 season, that distance has extended to over two miles. That hasn't made the rivalry any less heated, though.

The pair of matches between the sides in a Premier League season, known as Merseyside derbies, are always appointment viewing. Everton love nothing more than depriving their neighbors of valuable points.
If you love to get the upper hand on the folks next door, Everton will suit you nicely.
Connections between professional wrestling and football aren't difficult to find.
Former WWE star Sheamus is a huge Liverpool fan , while Drew McIntyre isn't shy about his love of Scottish side Rangers.

Premier League legend Wayne Rooney famously slapped Wade Barrett at a WWE Raw recording in November 2015, while Declan Rice and Mason Mount were filmed imitating Edge at an England training camp in 2021.

But All Elite Wrestling has the most significant presence in the Premier League as it stands. Company president Tony Khan serves as the vice-chairman and director of football operations for Fulham. In fact, AEW is the shirt sponsor for the Fulham women's team.
For those who have pledged their allegiance to the upstart wrestling promotion, the West Londoners are the logical choice when picking a football team to follow.

Hull City have returned to the Premier League for the first time since the 2016-17 season, earning promotion following a dramatic victory in the Championship playoff final.
However, the Tigers have never stuck around for more than two seasons in their previous trips to the top flight, and their last visit lasted only one.
If you like living on the edge and aren't scared of the prospect of your team dropping down to a lower division, the Yorkshire side could be worth a follow.
You're likely to see a lot of goals scored in Hull's matches; they just might not be coming from the team wearing amber and black.
That headline alone might have already cost us most of you. However, Ipswich Town are the team of the ginger song-machine's heart, and he's even a minority stakeholder in the club.
After the team's promotion to the Premier League in May, he was filmed giving an, erm, delightful rendition of his hit song "The A-Team" in the dressing room, along with the squad.
Sheeran's Mathematics Tour logo even donned the club's shirts for the last four seasons, although a new sponsor will be in place for 2026-27 and beyond.
So if you're a fan of the " Shape of You " singer, Ipswich could be a " Perfect " fit.

49ers Enterprises, the investment arm behind the San Francisco 49ers, took full ownership of Leeds United in 2023. That was the same year that the Niners lost the Super Bowl final to the Kansas City Chiefs, so read into that what you will.
Bad omens aside, Leeds successfully stayed in the Premier League last season after rising up from the league below, finishing in a comfortable 14th position.
The club is steadily building on that success with a handful of smart signings. A push into the top half of the table wouldn't be out of the question this time around.

Leeds actually won the last English top-flight title before the division was rebranded as the Premier League in 1992. While another trophy might be a while away yet, the club is clearly on an upward trajectory.
According to a 2025-26 Men in Blazers survey , Liverpool was named the top supported Premier League team among U.S. fans, picking up a hefty 22 percent share.
The club already has plenty of U.S. connections, with owners Fenway Sports Group also having the Boston Red Sox and NASCAR's RFK Racing under its umbrella.

But perhaps the most notable link is NBA legend LeBron James, who owns a stake in the team. The Philadelphia 76ers star is regularly seen donning Liverpool shirts and other merchandise, and he even launched a collaborative fashion collection with the club in 2023.
For fans of The King, rooting for Liverpool is an easy decision.

articles.title: Real Madrid y Barça, un inicio con cautela y freno de mano: "Al 30-40%, como mucho"
articles.standfirst: MARCA analiza junto a un especialista en control de cargas y prevención de lesiones en el fútbol de élite el arranque de los dos favoritos al título liguero y cómo el Mundial puede afectarles
articles.summary: MARCA analiza junto a un especialista en control de cargas y prevención de lesiones en el fútbol de élite el arranque de los dos favoritos al título liguero y cómo el Mundial puede afectarles
articles.body: Real Madrid y Barça vuelven al ruedo este fin de semana tras ausentarse de la jornada 1 que dio el pistoletazo a LaLiga EA Sports 2026-27. Una vuelta llena de asteriscos para ambos, pues el Mundial terminó el 19 de julio, la competición nacional arrancó el pasado 15 de agosto y los dos colosos de nuestro fútbol, cargados de internacionales que llegaron hasta las últimas rondas, empezarán con muchos de sus cracks 'justos' para la vuelta al cole. El calendario ya avisa de que este no es un inicio normal. Y para ello, MARCA ha querido aportar luz sobre el momento de forma en el que pueden llegar ambos -y también sus mundialistas- con un especialista en la materia. José Luis Felipe Hernández es catedrático de la Universidad de Castilla-La Mancha y sport scientist en la UD Las Palmas que también pasó por otros clubes de nuestro fútbol como Real Valladolid o CD Numancia. El especialista en el control de carga y la prevención de lesiones en el fútbol de élite, pone una cifra a la sensación que puede dejar este primer Madrid y este primer Barça: "Se espera un rendimiento muy bajo con respecto a las versiones que se esperan en marzo-abril, que es cuando ellos deben llegar al pico de competición con la Champions: un 40% como mucho". Y, para él, ni siquiera los dos parten del mismo punto. "En el Barça, que mantiene un poco más el bloque, el modelo de juego y todo eso, igual al 40%. En Madrid vamos a darle un 20 o un 30", explica, teniendo en cuenta además el cambio de entrenador y de dinámicas en el conjunto blanco. "Los que no han ido al Mundial han tenido cuatro o cinco semanas de vacaciones y después cuatro o cinco semanas de pretemporada. Estamos hablando de diez semanas... y los que sí que lo han jugado y han llegado casi hasta el final tienen una película completamente distinta", cuenta. El problema es que esas diez semanas no se pueden recuperar de golpe. El Mundial comprimió el calendario, la temporada está empezando y la propia competición se convierte prácticamente en una prolongación de la pretemporada. Por eso el aficionado puede encontrarse con una situación aparentemente contradictoria: un jugador que entrena, juega, parece encontrarse bien y, sin embargo, todavía está lejos de su techo. "Los sistemas de recuperación que tienen hoy en día los clubes y los futbolistas en su casas son increíbles y han cambiado mucho de aquí a cinco años atrás, pero no podemos pretender ver a un Vinicius a tope en la jornada 1-2", señala. Y, con esto, su recomendación es clara: "Hay que tener mucha paciencia y esperarle para la jornada 6-7, aunque al aficionado le cueste entenderlo. Los staffs lo tienen claro en este aspecto, pero claro... luego hay casos especiales y, yo entiendo que un entrenador eche la vista al banquillo si vienen mal dadas los primeros partidos y vea jugadores de la talla de Vinicius, Rodri, Mbappé... y se le pasen muchas cosas por la cabeza". Es una idea especialmente importante en dos clubes en los que la paciencia suele cotizar muy barata. El desgaste de un Mundial no se resume en los minutos jugados. Hay una parte evidente, los partidos de máxima exigencia, los descansos cortos, los viajes, el calor y los esfuerzos acumulados, pero también existe otra mucho más difícil de medir. "Lo que más les va a afectar ahora a los jugadores es en la cabeza”, sostiene Felipe Hernández. El futbolista pasa más de un mes fuera de casa, cambia de compañeros, horarios, rutinas y métodos de entrenamiento, no tiene su familia cerca y todo ello mientras compite por el título más importante de su deporte. "Todo eso lo metes en una coctelera y es una locura para una persona, sea deportista de élite o no”, resume. El contexto tampoco ayuda. "Han jugado partidos a 40 grados, yendo de una sede a otra, con dinámicas distintas a las que están acostumbrados durante la temporada, con otro cuerpo técnico, otros compañeros... y, claro, luego han jugado partidos a vida o muerte prácticamente un mes entero, un Mundial. Es una barbaridad", recuerda. "Vienen de partidos de élite al máximo nivel, al máximo rendimiento, con un calor increíble, mucha presión, jugándote mucho. Los jugadores se adaptan a todo aunque parezca una barbaridad, son animales competitivos", añade. Por eso el Mundial deja una mochila que no desaparece el día que el jugador se marcha de vacaciones. Aquí aparece una de las grandes batallas de los cuerpos técnicos durante las primeras jornadas: resistirse a utilizar a un jugador simplemente porque puede jugar. Y no es fácil, especialmente en Madrid y Barça, donde un mal comienzo puede generar ruido inmediatamente. José Luis Felipe lanza una reflexión que debería acompañar a cada decisión de los entrenadores: "¿Qué es mejor: perder un partido ahora en agosto-septiembre que no perderlo en abril-mayo?". La respuesta está relacionada con la planificación de toda la temporada, porque el objetivo no es acumular el máximo número posible de minutos, sino llegar al tramo decisivo en las mejores condiciones. "Que entrene menos ahora quizá es mejor, y que descanse más quizá sea mejor aunque, vuelvo a decir, a muchos les cueste entenderlo; a veces, menos es más", puntualiza. Jugar 90 minutos volver a jugar 90 y repetir puede parecer una demostración de fortaleza, pero también convertirse en un problema si el cuerpo todavía no ha terminado de asimilar el esfuerzo anterior. José Luis Felipe lleva una década trabajando en el entorno de los datos para utilizarlos y recuerda una frase que ha escuchado muchas veces: "Esto no es atletismo". Su respuesta a todos los que dudan de su trabajo es contundente: "Nada más lejos de la realidad, pero sí que hay puntos en común". El fútbol de élite también es correr, acelerar, frenar, repetir esfuerzos, trabajar la fuerza y recuperar. Y cada vez es más necesario medir todo ello: GPS para controlar desplazamientos y esfuerzos, plataformas de fuerza para analizar la fatiga neuromuscular, sistemas para controlar el sueño o la frecuencia cardiaca en reposo. Pero la pregunta que atañe a este momento, con el debut liguero de Madrid y Barça a la vuelta de la esquina y con algunos de sus jugadores 'al límite' casi antes de empezar, la pregunta es si realmente se puede saber cuándo un jugador está en riesgo de lesionarse. "La respuesta rápida es sí. La respuesta larga es no”, contesta: "Se puede controlar mucho, pero no todo". "Un futbolista puede pasar tres horas en la ciudad deportiva y otras 21 fuera de ella, pero... ¿Qué pasa en las 21 horas restantes? Ahí no hay control, ahí no hay GPS, ahí no hay nada y eso lo tienes que intentar adivinar”, explica. Por eso el descanso se convierte en un dato tan importante como los kilómetros recorridos: cómo duerme el jugador, cómo asimila el entrenamiento y cómo llega psicológicamente al día siguiente. "Los jugadores siempre juegan con fatiga, siempre juegan con estrés, siempre juegan con presión, por eso la clave para mí es el descanso. Si está durmiendo mucho y descansando bien, si está asimilando bien los entrenamientos... todo hará que la fatiga sea menor, y eso Flick y Mourinho, en este caso, lo saben bien”, recuerda. La cuestión no es eliminar la fatiga, sino evitar que supere el límite que el futbolista puede soportar. Pero, como es de esperar, todos los jugadores responden igual a una misma carga y el perfil físico es determinante para afrontar un inicio de temporada atípico como este. En el conjunto dirigido por José Mourinho,  el especialista José Luis Felipe  pone dos nombres especialmente bajo el radar con los que él tendría cuidado en estas fechas. El primero, Yan Diomande, por su carácter explosivo y por todo lo que rodea a su adaptación: nuevo equipo, nuevo país, enorme inversión económica y presión mediática. "Para mí sería un jugador a tener muy en cuenta en estos milímetros de los números, y no porque haya llegado lejos en el Mundial; es un jugador muy explosivo que repite esfuerzos de manera constante y a todo esto le sumas que ha cambiado de ciudad, de país, de club, un salto gigante en su carrera, ha costado mucho dinero... muchas cosas para alguien tan joven", apunta. El segundo es Jude Bellingham, por el tipo de futbolista que es, con mucha ida y vuelta y una enorme cantidad de acciones de alta intensidad: "Es un jugador al que creo que le cuesta recuperar y también le tendría bajo el radar", añade. En cambio, hay un jugador que le genera menos preocupación: Kylian Mbappé. "Es un animal competitivo y este muchacho está ya al 100%, no sé cómo lo hace, pero tú le ves y no parece que acumule en sus piernas todo lo que lleva, tanto de la temporada pasada como del Mundial con Francia", indica. Más allá de los nombres, el patrón que plantea José Luis Felipe es interesante. Los jugadores de banda y los perfiles explosivos suelen sufrir más: laterales, extremos e interiores que realizan esfuerzos de ida y vuelta a gran velocidad acumulan una cantidad importante de acciones de alta intensidad. Y aquí aparece una diferencia fundamental, ya en clave azulgrana. Rodri Hernández, reciente fichaje de los de Flick, puede recorrer muchos kilómetros, pero una gran parte de ellos son a baja intensidad. Otros futbolistas pueden recorrer menos distancia total y, sin embargo, someter a sus músculos a muchas más aceleraciones y sprints. “Creo que aquí la clave siempre está en la alta intensidad”, explica. Precisamente, uno de los jugadores a vigilar durante estas semanas sería el excentrocampista del City y capitán de la selección. Su llegada al equipo azulgrana combina nuevo club, nuevo entorno y ausencia de una pretemporada convencional, por lo que reclama prudencia con su incorporación al equipo. "Con Rodri hay que tener un poquito de paciencia con él, que aterrice, que esté tranquilo, que se ubique...", cuenta, reafirmando lo explicado anteriormente con la gestión de esfuerzos. "Él no va a hacer mucha alta intensidad realmente que pueda poner su cuerpo tan al límite como otras posiciones. Él llega para dar un posicionamiento táctico mejor al equipo, como hacía Busquets, pero no repetirá esfuerzos constantes como sí un Lamine", explica.  El segundo nombre es Pedri, no porque haya tenido una carga extraordinaria en el Mundial, sino precisamente por la necesidad de administrar sus esfuerzos con cuidado. "Precisamente porque tiene esa tendencia a lesionarse, como vimos en 2024, creo que ahora el Barça debe empezar a cuidarle poco a poco y a no correr riesgos. Es verdad que ha acumulado una barbaridad de minutos en verano -857 en el Mundial-  pero yo extremaría la cautela", justifica. La tecnología permite saber mucho más que antes. Los clubes pueden controlar la carga externa, la respuesta interna, la fatiga neuromuscular, el sueño y la evolución de cada jugador. Pero la información no sirve de nada si la competición obliga a ignorarla. A su juicio, la democratización de los datos también ha permitido competir mejor a los equipos con menos recursos. Todos tienen información de sus rivales y pueden encontrar la manera de hacerles daño. "Un equipo que no tiene la carrera de Mbappé o el regate de Lamine puede intentar encontrar en los datos la manera de neutralizarlos. Los equipos pequeños saben cómo le pueden hacer daño a los grandes a través de los datos, y por eso, entre otras cosas, ya no hay ligas de 100 puntos como antes... y cualquiera de puede pintar la cara", explica. El Madrid y el Barça parten con una ventaja que no necesita estadísticas para ser evidente: tienen futbolistas capaces de resolver partidos por sí mismos. Pero la élite ya no se puede permitir ignorar la información. "Son herramientas fundamentales, sin esto, hoy en día estás muerto", dice. Por eso, cuando Madrid y Barça salten al césped en estos primeros partidos, quizá la pregunta no debería ser si están bien o mal, sino cuánto de lo que serán capaces de ser en abril pueden enseñar ya en agosto. La respuesta de José Luis Felipe Hernández es contundente: todavía poco. Al Barça, alrededor del 40%; al Madrid, entre el 20% y el 30%. Lo demás tendrá que llegar con el tiempo, con minutos bien administrados y, sobre todo, con paciencia. Porque el Mundial terminó en julio, pero para ellos la temporada de verdad apenas está empezando.

Es una barbaridad", recuerda. "Vienen de partidos de élite al máximo nivel, al máximo rendimiento, con un calor increíble, mucha presión, jugándote mucho. Los jugadores se adaptan a todo aunque parezca una barbaridad, son animales competitivos", añade. Por eso el Mundial deja una mochila que no desaparece el día que el jugador se marcha de vacaciones.
